title: For Diwali, Houston Chef Anita Jaisinghani Shares the Traditions — and Her Besan Mithai
excerpt: The Pondicheri chef calls Diwali the ultimate family holiday, where sweets are good-luck gifts given with overflowing hands. Her besan mithai — a chickpea fudge — serves 12 and takes 55 minutes.
body:
• Houston chef Anita Jaisinghani, of Pondicheri and Indika, joined Houston Life for Diwali with a platter of mithai, calling the festival the ultimate family holiday.
  • She described sweets as good-luck tokens given away as gifts in overflowing hands — giving, in her account, brings return.
  • Diwali is a five-day Festival of Lights, held in mid-October to mid-November on the Hindu calendar, marked by colourful clothing and rows of diya lamps for light over darkness.
  • Her linked sweet recipe is besan mithai, a chickpea-flour fudge with ghee, cane sugar and cardamom: 55 minutes, serves 12, with an optional chocolate topping.

Chef Anita Jaisinghani brought a platter of mithai to Houston Life for Diwali, and called the festival the ultimate family holiday, likening it to Christmas, according to Click2Houston. Mithai — traditional Indian sweets — sit at the centre of how she describes the celebration: friends, relatives and neighbours visit, share meals and exchange sweets as good-luck gifts.

The traditions she describes

Diwali, the Festival of Lights, is described in the segment as one of the most important celebrations on the Indian calendar, signifying light over darkness. It is a five-day celebration held each year in mid-October to mid-November depending on the Hindu calendar, marking the beginning of a new year and a time to pray for a good, prosperous and healthy life. People wear colourful clothing and light rows of diya oil lamps and candles — the lighting is central enough to give the festival its name.

Food carries the social side of the holiday. Sweets are given away as gifts in overflowing hands, in Jaisinghani's description — a time of giving and celebration, where giving brings return.

From microbiology to Pondicheri

Jaisinghani was born and raised in India and initially pursued microbiology. She moved to the United States in 1990 and switched to food, taking her first cooking job in Michigan. She later moved to Houston, where she opened two Indian restaurants, Indika and Pondicheri.

Pondicheri opened in 2011; its menu is all-vegetarian and inspired by the diverse street foods of India. She has received four James Beard nominations in Houston. She said what she cooks is from memory, and that she likes making the food families eat at home rather than restaurant food — which is the spirit of the recipe she shared for the holiday.

The recipe: besan mithai

The sweet she points readers to is besan mithai, a melt-in-the-mouth chickpea fudge. Besan is gram flour made from ground chickpeas, and mithai is the general name for Indian sweets. The method turns on one patient step: toasting the besan in ghee with the sugar, cardamom and salt over medium-low heat, stirring constantly for 20 to 40 minutes until it is golden brown and nutty — the recipe warns not to leave it unattended, because it will burn.

Spread warm into a lined pan, it can be served plain or finished with a chocolate topping, pumpkin and sesame seeds, then chilled for an hour to set. Roasted hazelnuts, almonds or pecans can stand in for the seeds, and the page suggests serving it with kulfi or cut into bite-sized pieces alongside a dessert. It keeps in the fridge and can be eaten cold or at room temperature. The full ingredient list and steps are in the recipe card with this article.

steps: Grease a 9-by-13-inch sheet pan and line it with parchment paper.
If using the chocolate topping, melt the chocolate with the heavy cream over a double boiler, stirring frequently, and keep warm.
Heat the ghee in a large saute pan or kadhai.
Add the besan, sugar, cardamom and salt; cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until golden brown with a nutty aroma, 20 to 40 minutes. Do not leave it unattended.
Remove from the heat and immediately spread the mixture onto the prepared pan, smoothing it with an offset spatula.
If topping with chocolate, spread the warm chocolate over it, sprinkle with the pumpkin and sesame seeds, and refrigerate 1 hour to set.
To cut, let the mithai sit at room temperature for 1 hour first, and clean the knife with each cut.
